name: Nikhil Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy brake pads, filters, batteries and spark plugs for Redline Auto Parts, which supplies about three hundred garages. I lead two junior buyers, so mornings start with a quick huddle, then I check which parts are selling and which are sitting on the shelf. Afternoons are negotiations with parts makers and a lot of back-and-forth about delivery dates.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of it: stocking the right ten thousand parts out of two million possibilities. I also like helping the juniors get good. What wears me out is the pressure on margins and the worry about electric cars, which have far fewer parts to sell. My partner Priya is a dental hygienist, and we rent a flat near the ring road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent assistant, nothing more. At work I'd tell the juniors to use it for tidy emails and not for numbers. Online I'd probably roll my eyes at the hype and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm glad. A plateau means my job stays roughly as it is, and I'm good at it. What isn't fine is electric cars: if garages need fewer parts in ten years, my whole market shrinks regardless of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep my small habits, like asking a chatbot to tidy my supplier emails. I'd push Redline to widen into electric vehicle parts, like charging cables and battery coolant. And I'd keep saving a bit each month, about three months' worth by next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay. A little tense about the car market, but not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for, and how much do you trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it for emails and for summarising a long supplier report. I check anything with a number in it twice, because it once changed a price from 4.80 to 8.40 and I nearly didn't notice. So it's trusted for words, not for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most, if it isn't AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shift to electric cars. A petrol car has hundreds of parts that wear out, and an electric one has a few dozen. Garages tell me their brake and oil-filter orders are already down, and that hits my numbers directly.

say: It's a **decent assistant**, nothing more; I'd tell the juniors to use it for emails, not numbers.
Online I'd roll my eyes at the **hype**.
think: The job stays roughly as it is, which is good, but **electric cars** are shrinking my market anyway.
I'd rather Redline spent effort on the **real problem**, not on AI.
do: Push Redline to add **electric vehicle parts** such as charging cables and coolant.
Keep saving to reach **three months** of costs by next year.
feel: **Fairly okay**, tense about the car market but not about AI.
S0.quote: A petrol car has hundreds of parts that wear out, and an electric one has a few dozen.
fieldNote: Nikhil's unease is about the **electric car shift**, which already cuts garage orders, not AI.
He trusts AI for **words but not numbers**, after a chatbot changed a price.

steps.text: Keep tidying supplier emails with the chatbot and check every figure
Propose adding charging cables and coolant to the Redline range
Save enough for three months of costs by next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we should prepare, but not overreact. At work I'd propose a pilot on the boring tasks, like reorder suggestions, so we learn it on our terms. Online I'd probably stay out, but I'd talk about it with other buyers I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit worried. Buying is on the list. If reorder suggestions get good, Redline will want fewer buyers, and the first ones cut are usually the juniors, then people like me who are cheaper than a director.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the pilot, so I'm the one who knows the tool's weak spots. I'd take a course in data analysis, and spend an evening a week learning how the pricing models work. I'd also make sure my juniors are learning the same, because they're my team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. It's the feeling before a big exam when you know you can prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Redline to do for your juniors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A proper training plan, not a one-off. Hours on the clock, and a promise to keep the training roles open for a few years. If you lose juniors you lose the future of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where is the line between a task AI takes and a decision that stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The task is things like matching a forecast to stock. The decision is whether to trust a new factory or put money behind a trend. I'm the one who stands in front of the finance director and says why, and that's still a person's job.

say: It's real and we should **prepare**, but not overreact; I'd propose a pilot on reorder suggestions.
I'd talk it through with **other buyers** I know.
think: If reorder suggestions get good, Redline wants **fewer buyers**, and juniors usually go first.
I'm cheaper than a director, so I'm **not safe** either.
do: Volunteer to **run the pilot** so I know the tool's weak spots.
Take a **data analysis** course and teach the juniors alongside.
feel: **Anxious** in a useful way, like before an exam you can prepare for.
S1.quote: If you lose juniors you lose the future of the business.
fieldNote: Nikhil volunteers to run the pilot because the **owner of the tool** is rarely the first to go.
He frames the junior roles as the company's **future**, a point he repeats.

steps.text: Volunteer to run Redline's reorder suggestion pilot
Start an evening data analysis course
Teach the two juniors how the pricing models work each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mess and nobody is ready. Neither the government nor companies have a plan, and I'd say both are at fault for not thinking ahead. At work I'd ask the managing director for honesty about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose my job within a year or two of it arriving. A buyer is a thinking job, I'm senior, and that makes me expensive. My partner Priya's work is safe for a while, though, since you can't clean teeth by chatbot, and that's a big comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pull back on spending and hold off on any big purchase. I'd look for hands-on work in the car trade, like a service manager at a garage, since garages still need people. And I'd check what unemployment help there is, so I know it before I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a little sick, but I'd keep functioning. It would sit at the back of my head all day, like a bill I haven't opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first call you make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call Priya and then my old boss, who runs a garage chain. I'd ask if there's a role for someone who knows the supply side. It might be a weak plan but it's something to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think Priya's work gives you any breathing room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, yes. Her wage covers the rent and the bills, and my savings cover the gap. I'd feel guilty relying on it, but I'd be a fool not to.

say: It's a **mess** and nobody is ready; I'd ask the managing director for honesty about what's coming.
Both government and companies are **at fault** for not planning.
think: I'd lose the job within a year or two, since a senior buyer is **expensive**.
Priya's work is safe for a while, which gives us **breathing room**.
do: Cut spending and hold off on any **big purchase**.
Look for a **garage service manager** role and check what unemployment help exists.
feel: **Anxious** and a little sick, like an unopened bill at the back of my head.
S2.quote: My partner Priya's work is safe for a while, though, since you can't clean teeth by chatbot, and that's a big comfort.
fieldNote: Nikhil expects to lose the job but feels **held up** by Priya's secure work.
His fallback plan is **in the car trade**, using his supplier contacts.

steps.text: Hold off on any big purchase and cut eating out
Ask my old boss about service manager roles at his garage chain
Check the unemployment benefit rules before I need them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but there's time to do it properly. At work I'd ask for a joint plan on skills and I'd push for training. Online I'd keep it low-key and talk to friends instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's okay for me. I'd be thirty-two and could shift to hands-on work in the car trade or to work that sits closer to garages. The gap before robots gives me a runway, and I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a practical course, like a garage business or fleet management certificate, and keep my buyer job meanwhile. I'd test a side business supplying parts to a few small garages from home. I'd save more and keep learning the AI tools at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. Not calm, but there's a plan I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change careers with five years, or stay and adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both. I'd adapt at Redline for as long as it lasts and quietly build the side thing. If I'm in a good position when the job ends, I won't have to start from zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the two juniors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth: learn the tools, learn the garages and don't count on a desk job in 2031. I'd get them to visit garages too, so they know what a part really does.

say: It's serious but there's **time**; I'd ask for a joint plan on skills.
I'd keep it **low-key** online and talk to friends.
think: It's okay for me: I'd be thirty-two with a **runway** before robots reach hands-on work.
The gap lets me move towards **garage-side work**.
do: Take a **fleet management** certificate while keeping the buyer job.
Test a **side business** supplying parts to a few small garages.
feel: **Steady**, not calm, with a plan I can see.
S3.quote: I'd adapt at Redline for as long as it lasts and quietly build the side thing.
fieldNote: Nikhil's plan is a **bridge**: keep the job while building a side business that uses his supplier contacts.
He would tell juniors the **plain truth** and send them to garages.

steps.text: Take an evening fleet management certificate
Supply parts to three small garages from home as a side business
Save 300 a month towards a business cushion
Keep using the AI buying tools at Redline to stay valuable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and people shouldn't waste it. At work I'd suggest a skills plan for each buyer, reviewed once a year. Online I'd say governments should lay down rules early, so firms can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm pretty calm. By thirty-seven I'd be well on my way in something else, perhaps owning a small parts business. I'd also expect to have children by then, which makes me want something stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at Redline and grow the side business slowly. I'd save for a deposit and, with Priya, plan for a child around year four. And I'd keep the juniors learning, so that whatever happens they have a skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and optimistic. I like having a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good ten years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good ten years is one where I build something of my own that doesn't depend on one employer. That would suit me anyway, AGI or not. I've always wanted to run my own thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the state or the firm should carry the cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. Firms that save money from AI should fund retraining, and the state should set the minimum. If it's left to firms alone, small garages and small firms will get nothing.

say: Ten years is long, so I'd suggest a **skills plan** for each buyer, reviewed once a year.
Governments should **lay down rules early**, so firms can plan.
think: By thirty-seven I'd be well on the way to **owning a parts business**.
I'd expect **children** by then, which makes me want stability.
do: Grow the **side business** slowly while staying at Redline.
Save for a **deposit** and plan a child around year four with Priya.
feel: **Calm and optimistic**, since a long runway suits me.
S4.quote: A good ten years is one where I build something of my own that doesn't depend on one employer.
fieldNote: Nikhil turns the AGI question into the **owner's dream** he already had.
He wants **firms and the state** to share the cost, and worries small firms get nothing.

steps.text: Grow the parts side business to ten garage customers
Save for a flat deposit with Priya over four years
Plan a child around year four
Keep the Redline buyer job while the business grows

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, because I'd have no time to build the side business and no clear help from anyone. What would help is honesty from Redline early, a retraining grant that pays something while I study, and rules that force companies to share the savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people tend to treat buyers as numbers people. We're more like people who know where the supply chain breaks. That knowledge is worth something, and I'd like it to count.

headlineQuote: People tend to treat buyers as numbers people. We're more like people who know where the supply chain breaks.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of car parts who leads two juniors and lives with his partner Priya, a dental hygienist.
He uses AI **now and then** for emails, and trusts it for words but not numbers.
He is pragmatic, blames **slow planning** by both government and firms, and wants shared cost.
His mood goes **uneasy**, **anxious**, then **anxious** again at two years, and eases with time.
His plan is a **side parts business** that grows beside his job.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**: no time to build the side business and no clear help from anyone.
whatWouldHelp: **Early honesty** from Redline, a paid retraining grant and rules that share the savings.
